Where it began

Alec James Stewart was born in Merton Park on 8 April 1963. His father, Micky Stewart, had played Test cricket for England, so cricket was very much the family business. He went to Tiffin School in Kingston upon Thames and made his first appearance for Surrey in 1981, quickly earning a name as an attacking opening batsman who could also keep wicket.

The player

He and Nasser Hussain made their Test debuts together, in the first Test of England's tour of the West Indies that began in 1989. In 133 Tests between 1990 and 2003 he made 8,465 runs at 39.56 with 15 hundreds and 45 fifties, and behind the stumps he took 227 catches and made 14 stumpings. He captained England in 15 Tests.

The highlights came thick and fast. He made 190 against Pakistan at Edgbaston in 1992, his best Test score. In Bridgetown in 1994 he hit a hundred in each innings, 118 and 143, as England won there for the first time since 1935. As captain in 1998 he made 164 at Old Trafford to save a Test against South Africa, and England went on to take the series. Two years later, on the same ground, he scored 105 in his 100th Test.

What made him special

He did two jobs for most of his career, and sometimes three. Opening the batting he was fierce against the new ball, and Wasim Akram counted him among the hardest batsmen he ever faced. When picked purely as a batsman he averaged 46.90 in Tests. Keeping wicket as well brought that figure down, but it gave England a balanced side for years.

The one thing that slipped through his fingers was a Test double hundred. When he retired, nobody had scored more Test runs without one. It was not for lack of trying.

Away from the middle

Wisden named him one of its Cricketers of the Year in 1993. He was appointed MBE in 1998 and OBE in 2003, and the University of Surrey gave him an honorary doctorate in 2005. Surrey named the gates at the Vauxhall End of the Oval after him. He gave the club many more years off the field too, as ambassador, executive director and, from 2014, Director of Cricket, before becoming a part-time adviser in 2024.

And finally

A lifelong Chelsea fan, he wore the number 4 shirt in one-day internationals in honour of his boyhood hero John Hollins, and kept it for his whole career. In 2003 Michael Aspel surprised him with the big red book for This Is Your Life, catching him on a golf course, which was one way of making sure he could not appeal.
